root.note: bariyy / barrī. Wiktionary glosses it ‘savage’ and explains the sense as the outer, less built-up parts of a town; other references give ‘outer, exterior’. The Arabic origin is generally accepted, the exact meaning that was borrowed less so.

history: A bairro was first the part of town outside the walls. The word is Arabic, from barrī, linked with barr, ‘open land’, and it described the wild or outer areas, where the city thinned out. Over the centuries those outskirts became part of the city, and the word came to mean any neighbourhood. Lisbon is a city of bairros: Alfama, Mouraria, Bairro Alto, Graça. Each has its own life, its own café and its own festas in June. For people who live in Portugal the word also matters on paper. Your bairro is part of your morada, and the Junta de Freguesia that issues your atestado de residência covers your local area. Spanish has barrio.
historyEinfach: Bairro means ‘neighbourhood’. The word comes from Arabic. First it meant the area outside the city walls. Later it meant any part of a city. Lisbon has famous bairros: Alfama, Mouraria, Bairro Alto. Spanish says barrio.

cognates.note: a Spanish-speaking district in US English

elsewhere.text: Spanish barrio has the same origin and even travelled into American English.
In Arabic, barr is dry land or the open country, as opposed to the sea or the town.
